 Live .  13,484 viewing 13484 viewing Live page Updated 3 minutes ago Attacked Australian MP had both legs amputated, says husband
 Summary
 Phil Haines, husband of MP Helen Haines, confirms she has had to have both legs amputated 
 He added that the "good news" was that she was "alive and stable"
 Haines suffered severe lower body injuries on Monday when she was hit by a car 
 The man charged over the alleged attack, Brendan Nugent, has briefly faced court. Our correspondent Katy Watson was in the courtroom 
 Nugent, 43, did not apply for bail . He is due to return to court in February
 He has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official
 Police have not ruled out additional charges , including attempted murder

 Edited by Joel Guinto and Ayeshea Perera, with Katy Watson and Simon Atkinson in Wangaratta and Lana Lam in Sydney
 Cockatoo: Symbol of Haines' campaign published at 07:54 BST 07:54 BST 
 Simon Atkinson 
Reporting from Wangaratta 
 Image source, BBC/Simon Atkinson The orange cockatoo logos which are now displayed outside Helen Haines' office are a symbolofher election campaign.
 Her fortnightly newsletter is also called the Indi Cockatoo.

 'A moment for us to choose to be better', says governor-general of Australia published at 07:35 BST 07:35 BST 
 Australia’s Governor-General Sam Mostyn has spoken in the same press conference as Phil Haines.
 "This violent attack... must be a moment for us to pause, and to choose to be better," she says. 
 "We should do what I imagine Helen would be doing if she was not the victim of this terrible attack - reaching out to those who are terribly distressed by what has happened... to celebrate our strong and stable system of government and parliament and democracy, and be proud of that," she says.
 "Most importantly, that we learn or re-learn to exercise our muscle of decency," she adds.

 Five key points from Phil Haines' update published at 07:25 BST 07:25 BST 
 These are the main takeaways from the update by Phil Haines, the husband of Australian MP Helen Haines:
 The lawmaker has lost both her legs after the alleged attack
 But the good news is that she is alive, and "both her heart and her mind are in good shape" , he says
 Helen Haines' road to recovery will be "long and difficult" , but "she's a fighter", he says
 He thanked hospital staff and people, both in Australia and internationally, who have shown their concern for his wife
 He urges people who want to support Helen to make a donation to the Save the Children fund . "Please keep sending Helen your love," he says
 Image source, Reuters 
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 'Please keep sending Helen your love' published at 07:17 BST 07:17 BST 
 This was a "horrendous thing for our family, but we're very loving, very supportive", Phil Haines says.
 He also urged people who want to send Helen flowers or support her financially to instead make a donation to the Save the Children fund.
 "Please keep sending Helen your love, and our family as well" he says, adding that he has been advised by people to "take things day by day".
 Phil Haines has made his speech in a composed manner, flashing a smile at some points. But as he wraps things up, he looks emotional, appearing to choke up as he said a brief "thank you", before stepping away from the microphones.

 Haines' husband thanks hospital staff and community published at 07:13 BST 07:13 BST 
 Phil Haines goes on to thank the "many people who have been incredibly supportive" of their family in the last two days.
 He thanks Haines' office staff who were first on the scene, first responders, police, paramedics, and hospital staff who treated her.
 "I also want to thank the community, and across the nation, and internationally" for sending their love and support, he says.

 'Long and difficult' recovery journey ahead for Haines - husband published at 07:10 BST 07:10 BST Breaking 
 "Helen's road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter," Phil Haines says.
 "She is a determined person who will do her best, with our support and love, to recover. And that is what we hope for."
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Haines' heart and mind 'in good shape' - husband published at 07:06 BST 07:06 BST Breaking 
 "The good news in all this is that she's alive. That is the most important thing for our family," Phil Haines continues.
 He says the "two most important parts of Helen" are "her heart and her mind".
 He describes her as a "compassionate, caring, loving person" and with the "sharpest intellect".
 "We are grateful and thankful that at this stage, both her heart and her mind are in good shape."

 Haines 'alive and stable', husband says published at 07:04 BST 07:04 BST Breaking 
 "But the good news is that Helen is alive and stable," Phil Haines continues.
 "That's the most important thing for our family," he adds.

 Helen Haines has had both legs amputated - husband published at 07:03 BST 07:03 BST Breaking 
 After the "horrendous incident" that left Helen Haines severely injured, her left leg was amputated, Phil Haines says. As of this morning, her right leg has had to be amputated as well, he adds.

 Helen Haines's supporters continue to bring flowers at the doorstep of electoral office in Wangaratta, as she recovers from an alleged attack earlier this week.

 Helen Haines' husband to give update on her health published at 06:05 BST 06:05 BST 
 We've just heard from the Alfred Hospital in Melbourne, where Helen Haines is being treated, and which says that her husband will give an update on her health at 5pm - that's about an hour's time.
 Phil Haines will be joined by Sam Mostyn, Australia's governor-general, the hospital says.
 Stay with us as we bring you the latest updates.

 Watch: Helen Haines' alleged attacker appears in court published at 05:31 BST 05:31 BST 
 Brendan Nugent has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official.
 Media caption, What happened inside court for man charged with Australian MP attack

 Alleged attack on Haines 'unfathomable' - colleague published at 05:13 BST 05:13 BST 
 Image source, Getty Images David Pocock, an independent senator for the Australian Capital Territory and a colleague of Haines, has said that working with her is "one of the great privileges of serving in our parliament".
 The two recently worked on a petition to support students in allied health fields.
 Addressing the National Press Club in Canberra a while ago, Pocock said the alleged attack on Haines was "unfathomable".
 "We must meet this attack on you by doubling down on the values you represent: democracy, transparency, accountability, care, and kindness," he said.
 "Now is the time to think about what brings us together, to defend our shared values, our democracy, and our freedom to live as Australians."

 What do we know about the alleged attack? published at 04:48 BST 04:48 BST 
 The alleged attack happened outside Helen Haines's electorate office in Wangaratta, a city of about 30,000 people.
 Police said she was hit on Murphy Street at about 15:35 local time (05:35 BST) on Monday.
 Here is what else we know about the incident .

 Media caption, 'I'm not a hero': Man intervenes in Australian MP attack
 A Wangaratta local barber was among a group of by-standers who were first on the scene and detained the driver of the car that hit Helen Haines.

 Victoria Premier says Australia may be 'straying from the principles of our democracy' published at 03:49 BST 03:49 BST 
 Image source, Getty Images Ben Carroll, the Premier of Victoria, has said in a statement that what happened to Haines raised fears that Australia was "straying" from its democratic principles.
 He said he visited Haines's campaign office a couple of years ago and was struck by "a warmth you rarely ever find in politics".
 "Why would you attack someone who has spent her life making things better?" he wrote. "If you care about Australia, and the place we might become, today calls for soul searching."
 "And I genuinely fear that we're straying from the principles of our democracy. Respect. Equality. A fair go."

 Courtroom sketch of accused attacker Brendan Nugent published at 03:21 BST 03:21 BST 
 A sketch from Brendan Nugent's brief court appearance has just come through.
 Cameras and recording devices are banned in courtrooms in Victoria unless special permission has been granted to film proceedings.
 Image source, Reuters

 Albanese says he has spoken with family of Helen Haines published at 02:47 BST 02:47 BST 
 Albanese spoke to Haines' husband on the night she was rushed to hospital in Melbourne, where she remains in a critical condition, and on again on Wednesday morning.
 "We continue to engage and reach out to the family for whatever it is that they need, as well as [the] community that's really going through a traumatic period. This was not something that they would have anticipated and is a shock, I think, to all," he told ABC radio.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Women in politics targeted more aggressively, PM says published at 02:36 BST 02:36 BST 
 Many MPs have been talking about the threats they receive today, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese among them.
 But in an interview with the ABC, Albanese said it is particularly scary for women in politics, saying there is "a different form of vilification and aggression towards" them.
 "The nature of it can often be sexualised. I mean, threats of rape, unfortunately, something that most women parliamentarians can tell you they have received," he said.
 "That is shocking."
 Last night, Minister for Social Services Tanya Plibersek told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation she'd received countless death and rape threats in the almost 30 years she'd been in parliament.
 And just a day after the apparent attack, Plibersek said a stranger online had told her she “deserves to meet a Landcruiser” - the type of car used to run Haines down.
